why: The first thing every request meets. A loopback bind alone does not stop a web page in the operator's browser from posting to 127.0.0.1, so the Host header must be on the allowlist and any browser Origin must be same-origin.
name: guard

why: The single place roles are enforced. It resolves the session cookie, looks up the route the mux will actually run, and answers 401 or 403 before the handler sees the request. With no --auth-file it passes everything through.
name: authorize

why: One table decides who may call what. It is keyed by the mux pattern, so it cannot disagree with the router, and a route missing from it defaults to admin rather than public.
name: routeAccess

why: Password sign-in against a bcrypt users file. Failures are rate-limited per address and username, and success sets an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict session cookie.
name: handleLogin

why: The single-run lock. A second phase on a busy run, anything while the peer is stopped by a fault, and anything during a network reset are all refused here with the reason.
name: claim

why: Every phase route funnels through here: one running phase per run, bounded by the phase timeout, 202 returned at once and progress delivered over the event stream.
name: dispatch

why: Step 1's entry point. It validates the config, refuses on-chain mode when no Fabric network is configured, and runs the admission gates before any run folder exists.
name: handleGenerate

why: Every path that creates a run goes through these gates, so a second entry point cannot quietly skip them. A tier that cannot produce a trustworthy run costs nothing but the error message.
name: admit

why: Large tiers are refused until the 1, 10, 100 and 1,000-voter ladder has passed on this exact build. A console that cannot name its own commit is refused too.
name: ladderGate

why: Projects the ledger (on-chain) or the run folder (offline) and refuses a run that will not fit, with the numbers in the message. A volume it cannot read does not block the run.
name: diskGate

why: Projects the auditor's peak memory and refuses a run above what the host says is available. Hosts that cannot report it are not refused.
name: memoryGate

why: The single source of truth for a valid election. The UI mirrors these checks only for instant feedback; this is the gate every posted config passes.
name: Validate

why: Opens the run's journal with the environment snapshot, then shells the Rust generator. The Go layer builds an argv and does no cryptography itself.
name: Generate

why: Line 1 of journal.ndjson is the environment the run executed in: Go runtime, the saksi-demo version or hash, the commits of the generator and the console, the declared orderer batch, Docker, container limits, kernel and CPU. A probe that fails is recorded as null, by name.
name: OpenJournal

why: The saksi-demo gen entry point: parses the flags, validates the parameters, then writes the stream in chunks, or in a single pass with --chunk 0.
name: cmd_gen

why: Builds voters a chunk at a time, in parallel inside the chunk, and writes them in voter order before the next chunk starts, so memory is bounded by a chunk rather than the population.
name: write_election_stream_chunked

why: Everything that exists once per election: the parameters, the DKG transcript and the credential issuer's keypair. Every dealer polynomial and the issuer key come from OsRng, so no two elections share a key.
name: gen_prologue

why: One dealer per trustee, each drawn by Dealer::random. The generator's elections are published, so their secret key must not be derivable from this source.
name: random_dealers

why: A dealer's polynomial of degree threshold - 1, every coefficient from a CSPRNG. The constant term is this dealer's contribution to the election's secret key; before saksi #50 the generator used fixed coefficients instead.
name: Dealer::random

why: One voter end to end: issue a credential, then per position present it (the nullifier) and encrypt and CDS-prove one bit per candidate. It depends only on its inputs and its own randomness, so many run at once.
name: build_voter

why: How the realistic profile decides a race: a reserved share apportioned down the ranks, in integer arithmetic so the same parameters give the same population on any machine.
name: realistic_quotas

why: Which candidate a voter picks for a position. Deterministic from the voter index and the plan, which is what lets anyone regenerate the ground truth from the parameters alone.
name: select

why: Ground truth is counted from an explicit record of the selections, never as a side effect of building ciphertexts. That independence is what gives E = 0 its meaning.
name: tally_selections

why: Each trustee signs the published totals with a Schnorr proof of knowledge of its DKG share, which is what the chaincode's threshold gate and the auditor's tally.signatures check.
name: sign_tally

why: The plaintext tables of Appendix A. No cryptography runs here, which is why ground-truth mode reaches the 3.5-million-voter tier.
name: write_ground_truth_csvs

why: The data-validation gate before encryption. It streams the ballot table, so the capstone tiers audit in bounded memory, and writes its report into the run folder.
name: RunCheck

why: Recounts the ballot table from disk, checking each row's shape and voter ordinal as it goes, independently of the published summary.
name: recountBallots

why: Holds the independent recount against the published tally, contest by contest. This is the check the whole gate exists for.
name: compareToSummary

why: Step 4's entry point: loads the bundle and either drives the on-chain lifecycle to the close or records a local ceremony. Every outcome is stamped, so a failed start reaches run.end.
name: CeremonyStart

why: Builds bundle.json from the header step 2 wrote, pointing at ballots.ndjson rather than inlining ballots. The election is never regenerated mid-ceremony.
name: bundleFrom

why: Loads the cached bundle and returns a step function bound to this run: one ledger call, one receipt, one progress event.
name: lifecycle

why: The lifecycle prefix that must precede any trustee action: CreateElection, the DKG transcript, every ballot, then CloseElection, with the attack plan's pause points between them.
name: setupOnChain

why: The measured ballot window. Only submission and commit status run inside it; receipts, files and journal writes happen outside, so the numbers are the chain's.
name: submitBallots

why: The load driver: up to Concurrency ballots in flight, every result recorded, a dropped ballot counted rather than swallowed. Serial submission would measure the client, not Fabric.
name: Run

why: Submits one transaction and waits for its commit status, with no query call, which makes it the part of a submission that is safe to time.
name: Submit

why: After the window, fetches receipts one block at a time, so a thousand ballots in a hundred blocks cost a hundred fetches. A block it cannot fetch is stamped, not fatal.
name: collectReceipts

why: Fetches a block once and returns receipts for the given transactions it contains. The console reconciles anything missing against what it submitted.
name: ReceiptsForBlock

why: Writes a lifecycle receipt to receipts.csv and appends one line to trail.ndjson under the same lock. Append-only: the trail is never rewritten.
name: Lifecycle

why: Where the chaincode earns its place: decode, shape, the issuer's signature on the credential, the election open, the nullifier unspent, then every CDS proof, at endorsement. Each refusal names its gate.
name: SubmitBallot

why: Prefixes every refusal with gate=<id>:, a stable machine-readable name. The console reads it to say which check stopped an attack; a refusal by any other gate is not evidence about the one under test.
name: rejectAt

why: On-chain verification of the proof that a ciphertext encrypts 0 or 1, bound to the election, contest and nullifier. Byte-compatible with the Rust prover.
name: VerifyBinaryCDS

why: Fabric stores no block hash, so a receipt's hash is recomputed as SHA-256 over the ASN.1-DER header, exactly as protoutil does.
name: blockHeaderHash

why: Records the election parameters: version, a non-empty id, contests and trustees, threshold in range. An existing id is refused, which is also why a caller could front-run one.
name: CreateElection

why: Records the DKG transcript once per election, checking its shape and that threshold and trustee count match the parameters. It does not check that commitments are valid points; the auditor does.
name: PublishDKGTranscript

why: Records one trustee's share for one contest after the election closes: membership, shape, one per contest, and a Chaum-Pedersen proof that is present. The proof is verified off-chain.
name: SubmitPartialDecryption

why: Holds the lifecycle at a stage the run's plan lists until the operator runs or skips that stage's attacks, stamping each attack's mount context.
name: pauseForAttacks

why: Splits a security run's ballot window at the chosen fraction, mounts the ballots-stage attacks against the open election, then finishes. The halves are stitched back into one window.
name: pausedWindow

why: Submits exactly one trustee's partial decryptions. Every other trustee's shares stay untouched, which is what makes the threshold visible.
name: CeremonySubmit

why: The roster and the quorum. On-chain the ledger is consulted as the authority; offline the local ceremony file is.
name: CeremonyStatus

why: Groups the bundle's partial decryptions by the trustee id inside each protobuf rather than by array position, so a layout change cannot hand a trustee someone else's shares.
name: partialsByTrustee

why: Publishes the tally only once the threshold is met. Below it, nothing is submitted and the route answers 409.
name: CeremonyPublish

why: Keeps only the signatures of trustees who actually submitted, so the chaincode's count reflects the ceremony that happened rather than the full set the generator holds.
name: tallyToPublish

why: The chaincode's threshold gate: the election closed, one total per contest, no earlier tally, every signature valid and at least threshold distinct signers over these exact totals.
name: PublishTally

why: Rejects a tally carrying any bad signature, not only a shortfall, so the chaincode and the auditor can never disagree about the same bytes.
name: verifyTallySignatures

why: Checks a 64-byte Schnorr signature with a transcript identical to the Rust verifier, under a key derived from the DKG transcript alone.
name: VerifySchnorr

why: Step 6's body: dump and audit the ledger's copy, audit the console's copy, compare them, write correctness.csv, then decide run.end.
name: verify

why: Reads the chain's own record of the run into ledger/ and audits it with the same auditor. A dump that fails is recorded as not run, never as a verdict.
name: auditLedger

why: Pages through ListNullifiers and GetBallots, writing each page before asking for the next, and rebuilds a header from the on-chain parameters, DKG, partials and tally.
name: dumpLedger

why: Are the chain's record and the console's the same election? Same ballots by nullifier, same aggregate ciphertexts, both compared order-independently.
name: compareLedger

why: The audit-stream entry point: reads the header, opens the ballot stream without loading it, builds the thread pool from SAKSI_AUDIT_THREADS, and reports findings and timings.
name: audit_stream_dir_full

why: Verifies ballots in parallel batches, then folds findings, nullifiers and the aggregate serially in stream order, so the result is byte-identical to a one-thread run.
name: audit_streaming_chunked

why: Every per-ballot check: decode, shape, each CDS proof, the credential presentation and its issuer binding. Only a ballot that passes both proof families joins the tally.
name: verify_ballot

why: The double-vote check over a stream: one 32-byte key and a first-use index per ballot, nothing else retained.
name: NullifierTracker

why: Checks every trustee's Chaum-Pedersen proof against the aggregate the stream produced, and that enough distinct trustees contributed.
name: verify_partial_decryptions

why: The weight each participating trustee's share gets when the shares are combined at x = 0. Duplicate indices are refused.
name: lagrange_coefficient_at_zero

why: Combines the shares, recovers each total by bounded discrete log, and checks shape, range, the homomorphic sum and accuracy against ground truth.
name: verify_tally

why: Turns a plaintext point back into a count. The count is bounded by the number of ballots, so the search always terminates.
name: decode_tally

why: Baby-step giant-step: O(sqrt(max)) time and memory, used from 50,000 ballots up; below that a linear scan returns the identical answer.
name: bsgs_decode

why: Strict: no signatures is a failure, and so is any unknown or duplicated signer, any signature that does not verify, or fewer than threshold valid ones.
name: verify_tally_signatures

why: One self-contained row per contest: ground truth, decoded total, E, the recovered point, the aggregate it came from, and the artifact hashes, plus ledger rows on-chain.
name: writeCorrectnessCSV

why: Decides the run's verdict and stamps run.end, which is what campaigns, the runs list and summary.csv read.
name: Finalise

why: The failed-run predicate: a stage error, nothing submitted on-chain, a dropped ballot, a reconcile mismatch, any E not zero, or an interruption. The first clause that fires is the reason.
name: runFailed

why: The attack catalogue. Each entry names its lifecycle stage, its chaincode gate and its auditor check, and the briefing text lives beside the mutation it describes.
name: Registry

why: A simulated attack: audit the untouched copy as a positive control, apply the mutation, re-audit, classify.
name: runOneScenario

why: PASS needs the declared check among the auditor's failures. Something else failing instead is INCONCLUSIVE: the attack was caught, but not by the gate under test.
name: classifyAudit

why: PASS only when every gate id in the peer's refusal is the declared one. A refusal by an earlier gate, or one naming no gate, cannot be attributed and is INCONCLUSIVE.
name: classifyLive

why: Applies the mutation to a copy and submits it to the live election. The verdict is inverted: a refusal is the ledger doing its job, and an accepted tampered artifact is a finding.
name: mountLiveAttack

why: Checks the console and host against a planned run: Fabric, the declared orderer batch, the ladder, disk, memory, host load, audit threads and the phase timeout.
name: preflight

why: Starts a measurement campaign after preflight: warm-ups, measured repetitions, an optional sweep and burst. Attacks are forced off and one job runs at a time.
name: handleCampaigns

why: Runs the repetitions against the console's own API and writes summary.csv. A failed repetition is recorded, because the failure rate is one of the things a campaign reports.
name: Repeat

why: Raises the offered rate each step, over a fixed wall-clock window, until committed throughput stops improving or a ballot drops; the last good step is the plateau.
name: sweep

why: Runs 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 voters through the API and records ladder.json for this build only if every tier passes the gate with E = 0.
name: RunLadder

why: Rebuilds the Fabric network for a tier by running tools/tier.sh as a job. Admin, loopback and a typed RESET only, and never while anything else runs.
name: handleNetworkReset

why: Arms the peer-restart fault on an eligible on-chain run. Admin, loopback and a typed RESTART only; arming makes the run a security run.
name: handleFault

why: Stops the peer when the chosen share of ballots has been dispatched, keeps it down for the chosen time, and stamps the stop, restart and recovery in the journal.
name: newPeerFault

why: Decides from the journal alone whether a run can be resumed, before anything is dispatched, so a refusal comes back as a 409 with its reason.
name: planResume

why: Submits only the ballots the chain does not hold, then closes the election. A close that fails is retried by resuming again; one the chain already holds counts as done.
name: resumeAndClose

why: Reconciles the chain's committed ballots against the run and walks the chain, submitting nothing. Required after a node-restart test.
name: verifyOnly

why: The thesis export: every run's files, the journal, lifecycle receipts, summary and preflight in one zip. A file that cannot be read aborts the download rather than leaving a hole.
name: streamCampaignBundle

why: Public verification downloads. The name must match an allowlist exactly, nothing is served while the board is sealed, and the headers are streamed with ground truth and voter ids emptied.
name: serveBoardFile

why: The public board: results only after publish, turnout stated as synthetic, the check list, and ledger enrichment when a network is reachable.
name: buildBoard

why: Looks a tracking code up by nullifier prefix in the published ballots. An ambiguous prefix is refused rather than guessed.
name: handleVerifyCode

why: A signed-in trustee may submit only the trustee id in their session; any other id in the body is a 403.
name: handleCeremonySubmit

why: Tells an app who is signed in and as which trustee, or 401. With auth off the route does not exist, which the apps read as auth off.
name: handleMe

why: Serves the BalotaChain apps at /board/, /trustee/ and /admin/ from one folder, on the console's own origin, so the guard and the session cookie apply to them unchanged.
name: mountWebDir

why: The admin app's step 1: posts the form's ElectionConfig to /generate and returns the new run id.
name: generateElection

why: The admin app's step 3: posts /ceremony/start, which records the lifecycle and closes the election.
name: startCeremony

why: Posts /ceremony/publish. Below the threshold the console answers 409 and the app shows why.
name: publishTally

why: Chooses which wizard step an existing election reopens at, from its run status and ceremony state.
name: stepFor

why: Called on load. It returns the session, or null when the console answers 404 because auth is off; a 401 propagates, and the app sends the user to its login screen.
name: getMe

why: The trustee app's one write: submit this trustee's shares for the run.
name: submitPartialDecryption

why: The public board polls this every four seconds, which is how it flips from sealed to published on its own.
name: loadBoard

why: Checks a BC-XXXX-XXXX code's format in the browser, then asks the console whether a published ballot carries that nullifier prefix.
name: verifyTrackingCode

why: The election's terms as the chain holds them. Every later check — the contest ids, the trustee count, the threshold — is read from here, so an auditor never has to trust a local copy of the parameters.
name: GetElection

why: The public key material the ballots were encrypted to, read back from the chain. Exactly one transcript may exist per election, so there is no second key an auditor could be shown instead.
name: GetDKGTranscript

why: One ballot, addressed by its nullifier rather than by position. A voter holding a tracking code can be shown the exact bytes the chain recorded, without anyone having to vouch for a file.
name: GetBallot

why: Reads a page of ballots by nullifier so a whole election can be re-verified from the chain. A missing ballot comes back as an empty entry rather than a shortened list, so a gap can never be mistaken for a different ballot.
name: GetBallots

why: The committed set, paged. This is what makes the chain — not a local run folder — the authority on which ballots are in, and the mandatory pagination is what keeps that answer honest at a million ballots.
name: ListNullifiers

why: Each trustee's share, keyed by election, contest and trustee. An auditor can redo the threshold combination from the chain instead of taking the published tally's word for it.
name: GetPartialDecryption

why: The published result as the chain records it. Nothing here asserts the totals are correct — that is verified off-chain against the ballots — but it fixes exactly which totals were claimed.
name: GetTally

why: Open or closed, and nothing more. The trail treats it as display only: whether an election is finished is decided by a tally that reads back from the chain, not by this string.
name: GetElectionStatus

why: The one-way door. After it no ballot is accepted and threshold decryption may begin, and a second close is refused — the voting window cannot be reopened to admit a late vote.
name: CloseElection

why: The single decode path the write gates share. The parameters are re-read from state rather than taken from the submission, so a ballot cannot arrive carrying its own idea of the contests or the threshold.
name: loadElection

why: The check that decides a ballot came from a registered voter. It recomputes the Merlin issuance challenge and verifies the issuer's Schnorr signature over the credential commitment on the peer, so a forged or unsigned credential is refused at endorsement rather than discovered at audit time.
name: VerifyIssuerSignature

why: Walks a block range, checking that each block names its predecessor's recomputed header hash, and re-checks sampled receipts against the blocks as the peer serves them now. A fetch error leaves the status "not run", so an unwalked range can never read as a pass.
name: VerifyChain

why: The same walk with block fetching parameterised, which is how the linkage check is tested without a live peer. It holds two blocks of state rather than the range, so the check is the same at five blocks and at five million.
name: verifyChain

why: Height and current block hash straight from the peer's system chaincode. It is the anchor a stored receipt is compared against: if the chain has been rebuilt underneath a run, this is where it shows.
name: ChainInfo

why: Recomputes a receipt's block hash from the header rather than copying a hash someone handed over. That is what makes a receipt checkable later instead of merely quotable.
name: receiptFromBlock

why: What a client keeps as evidence a transaction committed: tx id, block number, and the three hashes that let the block be re-derived. The timestamp is the client's own proposal time, not consensus time — worth knowing before reading it as when a vote landed.
name: Receipt

why: The verdict of a chain walk. Status is never PASS unless the walk actually ran and both the linkage and the sampled receipts held, so a failed fetch cannot be mistaken for a clean chain.
name: ChainReport

why: One page of the committed set as the clients see it. The page size is pinned to the chaincode's own cap, so a client cannot ask for more than the peer will honestly return.
name: ListNullifiers

why: The chain-authoritative committed count, paged to the end. A run reconciles its submitted count against this, which is how a dropped or a double-counted ballot surfaces as a number rather than a suspicion.
name: CountCommittedBallots

why: Fetches a batch of ballots for re-verification. An over-long page is refused on-chain instead of quietly trimmed, and a short reply is an error here — a client never receives fewer ballots than it asked for without being told.
name: GetBallots

why: The clients' read of the election parameters. Every app that renders contests or counts trustees comes through here rather than through a local config file.
name: GetElection

why: How a client obtains the election public key it will verify ballots against — from the chain, not from the ceremony's own output.
name: GetDKGTranscript

why: The published totals as the clients fetch them. Whether those totals are right is settled off-chain by the auditor; this settles only what was published, and for which election.
name: GetTally

why: Why a transaction was refused, not merely that it was. The chaincode's own words and its gate=<id> prefix travel only in the gateway's error details, so without this a refused attack would be indistinguishable from any other failure.
name: ErrorText

why: The trail stays sealed until a tally is published. An operator may look early only from a loopback address and, with auth on, only with an admin session — so "nobody saw the result before the close" is enforced here rather than promised.
name: handleTrailAPI

why: Lists every election this console recorded, each one checked against the ledger. The chaincode has no ListElections, so this is the run store cross-referenced with the chain and not the chain enumerating itself.
name: handleTrailIndex

why: The entry point for running the attack catalogue over a run. It passes the same run validation, phase check and single-run lock as every other phase, so an attack cannot slip past the lifecycle it is meant to test.
name: handleScenarios

why: Assembles what the public trail shows, and fails closed. The gate is a tally read back from the chain, not the lifecycle status — the chaincode never sets a "tallied" status — and any read error keeps a non-operator sealed.
name: buildTrail

why: Turns the on-chain TallyResult back into contest and candidate counts against the recorded election parameters. It is the step between bytes on a ledger and a number a reader can check.
name: decodeTally

why: Serves the public copy of a run's verification records. Nothing beneath it may ever require a role, which is the only reason picking the file action off the path is safe here.
name: handleBoard

why: A single SHA-256 over every ballot's wire bytes in file order. It is order-dependent by construction: it fingerprints the ballot set as written, which is exactly why it moves when nothing but the order changes.
name: ballotsDigest

why: Binds each correctness row to specific artifacts — the DKG transcript, the tally, the ballot set — so a published result cannot later be re-attached to different inputs.
name: runDigests

why: Identifies which ballots a stream holds, independent of the order they were written in. The per-nullifier hashes are added modulo 2^256, so a million ballots cost one running total — and two directories differing only in order digest identically.
name: nullifierSetDigest

why: The SHA-256 of an audit's per-contest aggregate ciphertexts — the homomorphic sum the tally was decrypted from. It binds a verdict to the ballots that produced it, so two audits claiming the same result can be shown to have read the same ballots.
name: aggregateDigest

why: Runs each selected attack on a fresh copy of the run, never the source, and pairs it with a positive control that must audit clean. A scenario that passes because nothing was actually mutated cannot read as a green.
name: RunScenarios

why: Every scenario gets its own copy of header.json and the ballot stream. The original run folder is never touched, so an attack can never damage the evidence it is being judged against.
name: copyStream

why: Rewrites one field of a copied header.json. It re-marshals the whole object, so a clean-versus-tampered comparison has to be made field by field — the file bytes differ wherever Go's key ordering does.
name: mutateHeader

why: Flips one bit of a CDS branch response. The scalar stays canonical and nothing about the ballot looks malformed, so only proof verification can catch it — which is the whole point of the test.
name: tamperBallotProof

why: The double-vote attempt. The credential signature covers the commitment and not the nullifier, so the ballot passes every check up to the uniqueness one — which is precisely where it has to be stopped.
name: reuseNullifier

why: Sets a reserved protobuf wire type so the ballot fails to parse in every decoder, every time. A byte flipped at random would usually land inside a proof and re-test proof verification instead of the decode gate.
name: corruptBallotWire

why: Flips a bit of a partial decryption's Chaum-Pedersen response: a well-formed proof that does not verify. It tests that a trustee cannot pass off a share that does not correspond to its key.
name: tamperPartialProof

why: Flips the low bit of trustee 0's constant-term commitment. A canonical ristretto255 encoding has that bit clear, so the point stops decoding at all and the transcript is rejected before any ballot depends on it.
name: tamperDKGCommitment

why: Records each attack's verdict with the gate that was expected to refuse it beside the gate that actually did. A rejection by the wrong gate is not evidence about the gate under test, and this is where that distinction survives into the record.
name: writeNegativeTestsCSV

why: The admin app's run list. It reads /runs, a plain filesystem listing, so opening the app does not require the console to dial Fabric first.
name: listRuns

why: Asks the console what this deployment can actually do — on-chain mode, tiers, auth — before the UI offers it, so the app never presents a control the server would refuse.
name: getCapabilities

why: Reads the summary out of the exported election.csv rather than out of app state, so what the admin is shown is the same row an auditor downloads.
name: loadElectionSummary

why: The admin's only view of decryption progress: which trustees have submitted a share and whether the threshold is met.
name: loadCeremony

why: Asks the console to run its own verification pass over a run. The app computes no verdict of its own; it requests one and displays what comes back.
name: verifyRun

why: Pulls correctness.csv into the results view — ground truth beside the decoded total, with E the difference. A non-zero E is visible in the app, not buried in a file nobody opens.
name: loadCorrectness

why: Live progress over server-sent events. The console's hub drops events for a slow subscriber and has no replay, so this is a liveness cue and never the app's source of truth.
name: subscribeEvents

why: The trustee app's run list, deliberately reading /runs rather than the trail index: the index dials Fabric on every request and fails outright with no network.
name: listRuns

why: What a trustee sees of the ceremony: which shares are in, and whether the threshold is reached. It is polled rather than pushed, so a missed event cannot leave the app showing the wrong state.
name: loadCeremony

why: Asks the console to publish. Below the threshold it answers 409 and the app shows why, so a tally cannot be published by a minority of trustees.
name: publishTally

why: The auditor app's run list, reading the filesystem listing rather than the trail index so the public verifier still opens without a Fabric connection.
name: listRuns

why: Builds the download link for a run's artifacts. The auditor takes the same files the console published — the app is a viewer over the evidence, not a second source of it.
name: exportUrl

why: The original read-path bridge: it turns the chaincode's hex ElectionParameters and TallyResult into BalotaChain's bulletin shape, which is how the auditor view was first pointed at a real on-chain election. Superseded by the console's direct chain reads, and kept here as the record of that link.
name: BuildBulletin
